claims.text: At stage-1, OrderService.PlaceOrderAsync calls repository.AddAsync, then repository.SaveChangesAsync, then notifier.Send(order.Id, "order placed"), then returns the order; nothing catches an exception from Send.
OrdersController.Create awaits orderService.PlaceOrderAsync and only then returns CreatedAtAction (201 Created), so the response is produced after Send returns.

At stage-1, INotifier has one method void Send(int orderId, string subject), and the only implementation registered is LoggingNotifier (AddScoped<INotifier, LoggingNotifier>), whose Send is one logger.LogInformation call.
After SaveChangesAsync inserts a new entity whose key the database generates, EF Core sets the generated key on the entity, so order.Id holds the new row's id when Send is called.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Generated values (keys are set on the entity after SaveChanges)

claims.text: SaveChangesAsync commits the order (and its items) before Send runs; an exception thrown later by Send does not undo that insert.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Transactions (SaveChanges applies changes in a transaction committed before it returns); OrderService.cs:19-21 @ stage-1

claims.text: ExceptionHandlingMiddleware is registered first in Program.cs; it catches KeyNotFoundException (404), ArgumentException (400) and any other Exception, which it logs with LogError and answers 500 with title "Server error" and detail "something went wrong".
An exception not caught in an action method propagates out of the controller through the middleware pipeline to the middleware that wraps next() in try/catch.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Middleware / Handle errors (exception handling middleware placed first catches exceptions from later middleware)

claims.text: await releases the thread while the awaited operation is pending, but the code after the await (here: return order, then the controller's response) runs only after that operation completes.
claims.source_hint: .NET docs: Asynchronous programming with async and await (the await operator suspends evaluation until the task completes)

claims.text: Work queued with Task.Run runs on a thread-pool thread inside the current process; it is not persisted, so if the process ends before it completes, the work is lost, and nothing retries it when it fails.
claims.source_hint: .NET docs: Task.Run (queues work to run on the ThreadPool); ThreadPool threads are background threads that do not keep the process alive

claims.text: Sending a real email requires a network connection to a separate mail server, whose response time and availability the API does not control.
claims.source_hint: general: SMTP client talks to a separate server over the network (e.g. MailKit docs, SmtpClient.Connect/Send)

claims.text: Moving the email out of the request is preferable when the email is not part of what the customer is asking for, so the response should not depend on the mail server.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Background tasks with hosted services (long-running work outside the request)

claims.text: CancelOrderAsync at stage-1 has the same shape: it saves with SaveChangesAsync and then calls notifier.Send(order.Id, "order cancelled").

The exceptions a network failure raises in .NET (SocketException, IOException, TimeoutException) derive from neither ArgumentException nor KeyNotFoundException, so they reach the catch (Exception) clause.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference: SocketException, IOException, TimeoutException inheritance; ExceptionHandlingMiddleware.cs:16-30 @ stage-1
